item.title: Taylor Swift steals Emmys spotlight, watches husband Travis Kelce's Chiefs game with Tom Cruise
item.description: Taylor Swift skipped the 2026 Emmys to watch husband Travis Kelce with Tom Cruise, but still stole the show in a hilarious "SVU" spoof with host Mariska Hargitay.
item.content:encoded:
Taylor Swift skipped the 2026 Emmy Awards, but made sure to leave her mark on television's biggest night.

Swift, 36, still surprised the audience with a special appearance alongside her longtime friend and Emmys host, Mariska Hargitay, in a prerecorded "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit" spoof.

As the 78th Emmy Awards were underway in Los Angeles, the "Lover" singer was spotted chatting it up with Tom Cruise at Arrowhead Stadium while supporting her husband, Travis Kelce, at the Kansas City Chiefs game.

DOLLY PARTON, ROB REINER RECEIVE EMOTIONAL TRIBUTES DURING 2026 EMMY AWARDS

During the awards show, Hargitay joked about Swift and her fans during a skit featuring the cast of "SVU," where her character, Olivia Benson, wondered if Swift would show up to the Emmys.

TAYLOR SWIFT'S HUSBAND TRAVIS KELCE REVEALS WHAT REALLY HAPPENED AT THEIR ‘INSANE’ WEDDING

"Now, in order to crack a Swiftie case, you got to think like a Swiftie, because the Swifties think that everything is a clue to what she’ll do next," Hargitay said while navigating an evidence board.

As the team attempted to tie information together, a voice chimed in, "Hey guys, this isn't adding up."

Swift appeared from the back of the room wearing a blazer and matching slacks. "Our perp has a clear M.O.," she said. "A lot of this doesn’t fit the pattern, and I don’t think everything is a clue."

BRAD PAISLEY SAYS TAYLOR SWIFT AND TRAVIS KELCE THREW ‘ONE OF THE LEAST PRETENTIOUS WEDDINGS’ EVER

As the investigation played out, Hargitay determined, "Taylor Swift will not be at the Emmys."

Swift chimed in, "Maybe she’s going to do one of those cool pre-taped sketch things to support the host."

The camera panned toward the pair where the "Reputation" singer was shown holding her Scottish Fold cat named Olivia Benson, an homage to her favorite "SVU" character.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

While the feline may have brought them together, the pair have since enjoyed a flourishing friendship. Hargitay was featured in Swift's "Bad Blood" music video in 2015, and that same year, made an appearance at her tour stop in Philadelphia.

They were most recently spotted courtside wearing matching shirts to watch the New York Knicks during the NBA Finals.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"I was wearing a black T-shirt, and Taylor, being the prepared woman that she is, was like, ‘I got you,’ and basically handed it to me," the actress told Jimmy Kimmel recently. "I put it on, and that was the end of it."

Hargitay admitted she was "still floating from that wedding" after attending the couple's Madison Square Garden nuptials in July.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"It was so spectacular and so intimate," she said. "When there's a wedding with that many guests, you think, 'Oh, OK, it’s going to be that,' and it just wasn't."

She added, "And I even say that the vows were my favorite part of the whole wedding. It was that magical."

While Swift's spot aired from the West Coast, she sat comfortably with Cruise in the Midwest for Kelce's season opener against the Denver Broncos.

The "Mission Impossible" star previously supported Swift during the second night of her Eras Tour stop at Wembley Stadium in London, where Cruise was spotted trading friendship bracelets with fans – a fan-favorite tradition.

Their appearance at Arrowhead Stadium Monday also marked Swift's first Chiefs game as a married woman.

Swift and Kelce married on July 3 in front of 1,000 guests at Madison Square Garden, a representative for the pop star told Fox News Digital. The pair opted out of a traditional wedding party, and instead choose Swift's brother as her "Man of Honor" and Kelce's brother as his "Best Man."

Swift's representative revealed to Fox News Digital that the couple's wedding ceremony looks were designed by Jonathan Anderson of Christian Dior Haute Couture. The happy couple both wore white, and the "Life of a Showgirl" singer accessorized with Cartier.

Fox News Digital's Lauryn Overhultz contributed to this report.

item.title: Newsom roasted online for 'staged' fly-fishing interview with CNN anchor where he dropped major 2028 hint
item.description: California Gov. Gavin Newsom's fly-fishing interview with Jake Tapper in Montana sparked social media mockery, with users calling the CNN outing staged.
item.content:encoded:
Social media users are taking jabs at California Gov. Gavin Newsom over his latest political stunt — a recorded fly-fishing outing with a CNN anchor that the Democrat used to break news about his often-rumored presidential ambitions.

In the interview, recorded in Montana more than a month ago, CNN's Jake Tapper is seen with Newsom standing in shallow water, repeatedly casting fly reels while talking politics. Newsom told Tapper he wouldn't run for president if former failed 2024 presidential candidate former Vice President Kamala Harris tossed her hat into the ring.

"Of course not. Why would I?" Newsom said when asked whether he would run against Harris in a presidential primary. "I wouldn’t do that to her. I wouldn’t do it to me. Why would I? I wouldn’t do that to you."

"I wouldn’t waste everyone’s time. Who needs that?"

JENNIFER SIEBEL NEWSOM DODGES QUESTION ON HUSBAND GAVIN'S PRESIDENTIAL ASPIRATIONS

Tapper pushed back, saying Newsom could do it if he really wanted to.

But the Golden State governor replied by saying that would be a "gift from God for everybody else," likely referencing those who don't want to see a Democrat win in November, and claimed a primary against the former nominee would be "mutually assured destruction."

"I know her base of supporters. I know her friends," Newsom said of the former U.S. senator from California.

"The zen diagram (sic) on that is just pure crossover. It’s not — I wouldn’t do that to — I wouldn’t do that to people," he said, mixing up the Buddhist meditation practice with a Venn diagram, the visual tool where overlapping circles are used to show how groups are similar and different.

KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY

On social media, the reactions to the video widely shamed the pair for a stunt that was viewed as contrived.

"why [sic] is newsom fly fishing in business casual?" an X user named Sam Alberti asked.

"How lucky are we that a camera crew just happened to be standing in a Montana river while two guys who can’t cast pretended to fly fish," said a popular X user with more than 55,000 followers. "Totally organic. Not staged at all. CNN is doing the Lord’s work trying to make Newsom look like a regular dude. Herculean task.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​"

Free Beacon reporter Chuck Ross wrote, "The best part of this is when Newsom says 'Zen diagram' when he was talking about a Venn diagram."

"Jake Tapper and Gavin Newsom pretending to be regular guys fishing is absolutely hilarious," said another user with 1.7 million followers.

'HE'S SO THIRSTY': NEWSOM'S 'ENTHUSIASTIC' PRAISE FOR TRUMP POLICY TURNS HEADS

"This is the most Gavin Newsom-ish fishing video ever -- the French Laundry of fishing!" said politico Kenneth Baer, referring to the upscale California restaurant where Newsom dined with a group of friends during COVID-19 lockdown despite his implementation on state-wide restrictions on social gatherings during the pandemic.

"'Let’s do this interview surrounded by an entire film and sound crew in the river. Yeah, yeah, that’ll make us seem like nature guys,'" economist Nick Messenger said sarcastically.

Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office but did not hear back by time of publication.

item.title: Newt Gingrich reflects on what sets Trump apart from other leaders at GOP midterm convention
item.description: Newt Gingrich says Trump "has no boundaries" and is "not editable" in a Hannity podcast conversation taped at the Republican midterm convention.
item.content:encoded:
Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich offered a candid assessment of what sets President Donald Trump apart from other politicians, describing his unfiltered nature as both an asset and a liability.

"He has no boundaries," Gingrich said during a "Hang Out With Sean Hannity" podcast episode taped at last week's Republican midterm convention in Dallas.

"It's good, and it's bad..." he continued. "He's totally authentic. Now the problem with that is he's not editable because he's totally authentic."

JD VANCE REVEALS TRUMP'S 'UNBELIEVABLE ABILITY' THAT BEHAVES LIKE A 'SPIRITUAL DIMENSION'

Gingrich made the remarks after Hannity asked what sets the president apart from other leaders, prompting the former House speaker to reflect on a president he has known for years.

During the discussion, the former speaker also pointed to Trump's wide-ranging areas of focus and his tendency to move quickly from one issue to another, noting recent actions involving space policy.

TRUMP CALLS ISS CREW FROM HOUSTON TO PRAISE SPACE PIONEERS AND OFFER 'OVAL OFFICE TIME'

"He's interested in everything..." Gingrich said. "He puttered along for a while, and he suddenly, bam, [he] did a bunch of very decisive, very important things, and now he's off doing something else."

In recent weeks, Trump signed a new national space transportation policy aimed at expanding U.S. launch capacity and issued an executive order creating a commission to develop a proposal for a NASA-led U.S. Space Academy.

Gingrich has been a prominent supporter and ally of the president since his first term, frequently offering favorable assessments of his style, policies and approach to governing. He wrote extensively about Trump's rise during the 2016 campaign and has authored books examining his presidency.

His latest assessment came as Republicans gathered for the party's first-ever midterm convention, where Trump and Vice President JD Vance addressed party members as the GOP works to retain its congressional majorities for the remainder of Trump's second term.

Gingrich's full conversation with Hannity is available on iHeartRadio, YouTube, Spotify, Apple Podcasts or wherever you get your podcasts.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy judge indefinitely impounds juror names, citing safety and 'divisive' attention
item.description: Judge William Sullivan sealed juror names in the Lindsay Clancy mistrial case, citing safety concerns and unauthorized identification of jurors.
item.content:encoded:
The judge in the Lindsay Clancy case has indefinitely sealed the jurors' names, citing safety concerns and what he called "significant and divisive attention" on the trial.

Judge William Sullivan issued the order on Monday and said while the court acknowledges that the jurors' names must be made available to the public, there is a "real and present" risk of harm to the jurors, stating he's impounding all names indefinitely until otherwise ordered.

Sullivan noted that there have been "identifications of jurors and their personal information without their permission" in explaining his reasoning for shielding the jurors' names.

"Some of the empaneled jurors have come forward and spoken to the media after the declaration of a mistrial on September 4, 2026. However, the majority of the jurors, deliberating and alternates, have maintained their anonymity, despite multiple requests to give statements," Sullivan wrote. "The Court concludes that there is a risk of immediate and irreparable injury should the list be made available to the public at this time."

LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR DENIES BIAS ALLEGATIONS, WANTS 'CONVERSATION STARTED' ABOUT WOMEN'S MENTAL HEALTH

Clancy, 36, faced three counts of first-degree murder in connection with the slayings of her children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan — who were discovered strangled at the family's home in January 2023. Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial on Sept. 4 after jurors could not agree on a unanimous verdict, with the panel split 11-1.

One of the jurors, Paula Devlin, 65, denied allegations of bias when speaking with Fox News Digital.

"We didn't know what was going on outside of that room, but we knew that we had a chance to get a conversation started that could change something, that could maybe stop this from ever happening again," Devlin said. "I think that's one of the reasons why we feel — or I feel — so strongly about this is that I hope that no other woman or husband has to go through this."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Devlin said there were "holes" in the prosecution's case after reviewing the evidence.

"In the biggest piece of the whole case, the whole thing was based on mental health. How can you have bias if only women can go through postpartum depression? Only women can go through postpartum psychosis. Only women can deliver a baby. That's not biased. That's just a fact," she said.

Clancy is due back in court on Sept. 29 for a status hearing, at which more information about the future of her case may be revealed. The Plymouth County District Attorney's Office hasn't made a decision on whether the case will be retried.

item.title: Army veteran paratrooper who deployed to Iraq, Afghanistan before helping rescue Fox News reporter dead at 50
item.description: Sean Michael Lee's cancer was linked to burn pits in Iraq and Afghanistan, ending a life devoted to rescuing thousands from war zones and disasters.
item.content:encoded:
Sean Michael Lee, an Army paratrooper who helped evacuate thousands from conflict zones after his service — including Fox News' Benjamin Hall — died Sunday after a battle with esophageal cancer.

Lee was a 20-year veteran of the Army, having served multiple deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan as a member of the Army's storied 82nd Airborne Division, according to his obituary.

"He was, to his core, a paratrooper. Long after he took off the uniform, the values forged there remained the organizing principles of his life: duty, loyalty, competence under pressure, and an unwavering commitment to the person beside him," his obituary reads.

AMERICA’S PROMISE TO OUR AFGHAN ALLIES IS STILL UNFINISHED FIVE YEARS LATER

Lee spent the years after his military service continuing to help people. In 2021, as Afghanistan's government was collapsing, Lee worked to help evacuate thousands during a chaotic withdrawal as a member of the nonprofit group Save Our Allies.

Just a year later, Lee was in Poland helping deliver supplies to the frontline in Ukraine in the midst of Russia's invasion. It was there that Lee became a key part of extracting Fox News correspondent Benjamin Hall, who had been severely injured when Russian forces attacked his vehicle near Kyiv. Two members of Hall’s crew were killed in the attack.

BENJAMIN HALL TACKLES GRUELING ONE WORLD TRADE CENTER CLIMB ON PROSTHETIC LEGS TO HONOR FALLEN HEROES

"We got the call, we had just finished up a staff meeting with our folks back in the United States, and I can tell you that in about 90 minutes our guys were out the door and on the way," Lee explained to the Daily Caller during a 2022 interview.

Lee also worked to help wounded veterans through The Independence Fund.

In 2024, Lee helped deliver life-saving supplies to survivors of Hurricane Helene in North Carolina. He lived out of a tent in the Tar Heel state as he helped deliver aid to communities where support systems had collapsed, according to his obituary.

LUKE COMBS AND ERIC CHURCH RAISE OVER $24.5 MILLION FOR HURRICANE VICTIMS AT STAR-STUDDED CONCERT FOR CAROLINA

Most recently, Lee had been working under Secretary Doug Collins at the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs.

He was part of the U.S. military's 2003 invasion of Iraq. He was also part of the storied Bravo Company in the 2-508 Parachute Infantry Regiment. Half of the company received Purple Hearts for an Afghanistan deployment that was documented in Ben Kesling’s book "Bravo Company: An Afghanistan Deployment and its Aftermath."

Lee's two best friends — Sgt. Michael Verardo and Sgt. Allen Thomas — both of whom deployed with him to Afghanistan, passed away before him.

Lee's cancer was the direct result of his exposure to the burn pits in Iraq and Afghanistan. He died at age 50.

VETERANS FACE SURPRISING THREAT AFTER CANCER DIAGNOSIS, STUDY REVEALS

"I can’t even begin to explain what the world has just lost," former MMA fighter and Special Forces sniper Tim Kennedy wrote in a post on Instagram.

"This country has lost one of the finest men ever to serve it," Kennedy's message continued.

"Sean redefined the word service. He did not just volunteer to put on the uniform and join the 82nd Airborne. He dedicated his entire life to other people. He put his life on the line more times than anyone can count. Wherever people needed help, you found Sean. Whenever I needed help, I found Sean," Kennedy wrote.

Lee's life "cannot be measured simply in years, deployments, jobs, or missions. It is measured in people who made it home because he went toward danger," his obituary, shared by Heritage Funeral & Cremation Services, says. "In wounded men carried to safety. In Afghan families given a chance to begin again. In communities that received help when they believed they had been forgotten. In veterans whose lives were better because he continued serving them after his own time in uniform ended. And in the children who simply knew him as Uncle Sean: the constant, fiercely protective man who showed up."

Fox News Digital contacted Save Our Allies for comment.

item.title: Europe’s left courts Muslim voters as anti-Israel politics reshape continent
item.description: Europe’s far left is finding common ground with Islamist-linked networks on anti-Israel politics, creating a growing challenge for Jewish communities and voters.
item.content:encoded:
It's known as the "Red-Green Alliance" — a political coalition between Europe's far-left parties and Islamist groups that is increasingly shaping policy, particularly regarding Israel as the continent experiences a worrying rise in antisemitism that critics are linking to this partnership. 

With the rise of Muslim voters across Europe, many on the left and extreme-left are being influenced by this increasingly important voting bloc. 

Just last week in the U.K., critics accused the left-wing Labour government of sanctioning Israel as a ploy to win back Muslim voters from the far-left, anti-Israel Green and Independent parties. Conservative lawmaker Tom Tugendhat called the sanctions' announcement "performative politics."

In Sunday’s parliamentary elections in Sweden, exit polling from the state broadcaster shows that votes from non-European Swedes are giving an alliance of left-wing parties a narrow three-seat lead over a right-leaning coalition led by current Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson.

GERMAN OFFICIALS WARN ISLAMIST, FAR-LEFT RHETORIC DRIVING SPIKE IN ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS

One Swedish political researcher, Tobias Hübinette, pointed to Mayor Zohran Mamdani's win in New York City and said that the numbers in the Swedish election show that this "election meant a 'Mamdanification' of urban Sweden, and the gap between city and country is now larger than ever before," he wrote on X.

"They should be in disagreement," Simone Rodan-Benzaquen, the senior envoy to Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies told Fox News Digital, "but the Islamists are very capable of covering that up for political purposes… The antisemitism that we have today, in particular in Western Europe, is definitely fed far more (by) the far left's discourse."

Alan Mendoza, executive director of the Henry Jackson Society in the U.K. said that, "For a decade, Europe has trained its anxieties almost exclusively on the far-right, and while that vigilance is warranted, it has left a blind spot on the other flank… Antisemitism is not less dangerous because it arrives waving a progressive banner."

Germany-based Dresden University of Technology research fellow Janek Treiber said that, "There is indeed an intriguing alliance between the supposedly progressive Left and regressive forces within Islamism." He told Fox News Digital that, "The unifying factor is a kind of victimization narrative. For the Left that supports the Palestinian cause, Muslims are the oppressed and the West – including Israel – are the oppressors… Whether Muslims hold conservative-religious views in this context is irrelevant."

ANTI-MIGRANT AFD SEEKS TO BREAK GERMANY’S POLITICAL ‘FIREWALL’ IN HISTORIC STATE ELECTION

Voters in Berlin head to the ballot box this coming Sunday, with polls showing the far-left Die Linke party, literally translated as the "The Left", leading the center-right Christian Democratic Union by two points.

"In Berlin, a party polling at the top of the field has factions that share platforms, demonstrations and slogans with networks the German security services themselves link to Hamas and the PFLP," Mendoza claimed. "When 'Death to the IDF' and 'Intifada' are chanted at an election event, and the response from parts of the party is to defend the man who led them, the red line has been erased, not crossed."

Rodan-Benzaquen says that while Germany’s political "firewall" against far-right parties like the AfD "seems to work more or less on the right, it doesn't on the left," because, "there is a perception that whatever comes from the left, even the far-left, is not morally as repugnant as anything that comes from the right."

ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS

Germany and the U.K. are not alone. The far-left Sumar party in Spain is part of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s ruling coalition. Their support in the last election was strongest in areas with high Muslim populations, with party members attending demonstrations with Muslim Brotherhood-adjacent groups and Gaza protests organized by Islamist-leaning networks. Members have also pushed for Spain to recognize a Palestinian state while also referring to Israel as an "apartheid state." Spain recognized a Palestinian state in 2024.

The far-left La France Insoumise (LFI) party in France has been accused by academics and ministers of "Islamo‑leftism" after their de facto leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, refused to call Hamas a terrorist organization and party members marched with Islamist-linked NGOs during Gaza protests. The LFI’s popularity has been on the rise in polling ahead of next year’s presidential election and, according to French newspaper Le Monde, the LFI’s electoral strength lies in Muslim-majority suburban districts.

The Israeli Ambassador to France, Joshua Zarka, recently told Fox News Digital that, "The way [LFI leader] Jean-Luc Mélenchon speaks in front of a crowd reminds me of Hitler. The way he uses the idea of uniting against one enemy by speaking of Israel is similar to the way Hitler used to speak about the Jews."

Commenting on the sanctions imposed by the U.K. government on Israel, Britain's Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis called the announcement on X "a truly dark day for British Jews." His statement continued in part, "Gesture politics of this kind feeds into an increasingly hostile discourse about Israel," he wrote, warning that the cumulative effect of such policies could "further embolden those, at home and abroad, who use hatred as a weapon against Jews."

EXILED MUSLIM SCHOLAR WARNS FAR-LEFT–ISLAMIST ALLIANCE BEHIND ANTI-ISRAEL PROTESTS ECHOES IRAN’S RISE

Pointing to the U.K., Rodan-Benzaquen said the alliance grew while Jeremy Corbyn was the Labour Party leader. "You have this far left anti-imperialist, anti-colonialist, opposition to American power and, of course, to Israel itself. An alliance with Islamist organizations and movements that sort of adopt a common language, despite the fact that on many topics they are in certain disagreement… They have basically turned themselves from a party that cared about class, that cared about improving (lives), social rights, etcetera, into a party that is basically looking at identity politics and is trying to appeal to certain voters."

She said the red-green alliance is nothing new. "We've seen it for a long time. We've actually seen it in the Islamic Republic of Iran when the Islamic Revolution happened."

Europe’s Muslim population is estimated to be 45–46 million, up by 15.9% from 2010, based on Pew Research Center projections. That same study revealed the population of European Jewry had fallen to under 1.3 million — down 8% from 2010. 

Rodan-Benzaquen says of European Jews, "electorally, we don't weigh," so they have again become a political football. She says when left and far-left parties say, "Oh, we want to fight against antisemitism. The only reason why they're saying it is because it's a tool to attack the far-right."

item.title: China expert warns Beijing wants Americans — not the CCP — to spread its message
item.description: A China expert testifying before Congress says Beijing uses American organizations as "Trojan horses" to make its influence appear homegrown.
item.content:encoded:
Congress will examine how foreign adversaries — particularly China — seek to influence American public opinion and policymaking at a hearing in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday.

One of the expert witnesses told Fox News Digital ahead of the hearing that Beijing's greater advantage lies in shaping debate inside the United States through American organizations rather than direct Chinese propaganda.

Matthew Johnson, a China expert and senior fellow at the Jamestown Foundation, said Beijing increasingly seeks to influence debates over national security and other strategic issues by working through American institutions and organizations, making its messages appear homegrown rather than directed by the Chinese government.

HOUSE PANEL TO PROBE FOREIGN ‘TROJAN HORSES’ AS SINGHAM SCRUTINY WIDENS

"The idea is that it's not the Communist Party talking, it's actually institutions and individuals in the United States who are talking," Johnson told Fox News Digital. "That's actually the best outcome because then it looks organic... it looks like it's somehow being produced from within our society as opposed to by external actors."

Johnson said one of Beijing's current priorities is slowing U.S. advances in artificial intelligence and data-center infrastructure—an area he said Chinese leaders view as central to strategic competition with the United States. He said China's influence strategy combines grassroots activism with efforts to shape thinking among academics, policy experts and other influential voices.

His testimony comes as Congress continues examining the funding network linked to Shanghai-based Marxist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham, whose nonprofits have become the subject of congressional investigations and a federal criminal probe.

Fox News Digital previously reported that Singham directed at least $285 million into six pro-China, pro-communist nonprofit organizations beginning in 2017, including CodePink. Singham and the organizations have denied taking direction from the Chinese government, and neither Singham nor the organizations have been charged with wrongdoing.

HOUSE PANEL SUBPOENAS 3 LEFT-WING GROUPS IN PROBE OF $39M TIED TO MARXIST TYCOON NEVILLE SINGHAM

Johnson is scheduled to testify Tuesday before the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia, which will hold a hearing titled "Trojan Horses: Covert Foreign Malign Influence Operations in America." Lawmakers are expected to examine how foreign adversaries, including China, Cuba and Iran, may use nonprofits, activist networks and other organizations to shape U.S. public opinion and policy.

"My goal is to raise the curtain to expose these operations and stop them from undermining our national security, capitalism and the American Dream," committee Chairman Rep. Bill Huizenga, R-Mich., told Fox News Digital.

Johnson said the hearing focuses on what lawmakers describe as "malign foreign influence"—efforts by foreign governments to shape American public debate and policymaking by steering conversations toward their own strategic interests rather than those of the United States.

"I try to break down influence in terms of looking at ways in which the framework of very sensitive strategic conversations is being steered in ways that seem to map onto China's strategic interests, not American strategic interests," Johnson said.

He said the concept of a "Trojan horse" reflects Beijing's preference for influencing American debate through domestic institutions and individuals rather than direct government messaging.

"From an American perspective, we want to be sure that it's Americans who are leading the debate on this issue, not Beijing," Johnson said.

CHINA’S INFLUENCE MACHINE: FEDERAL RECORDS EXPOSE BEIJING’S PUSH TO SWAY AMERICA

Among the organizations that have received funding from Singham's network is CodePink, the anti-war activist group co-founded by Medea Benjamin and Jodie Evans, Singham's wife. CodePink has spent years organizing disruptive protests inside Congress, campaigning against U.S. policy toward China, Cuba and Israel, and promoting its "China Is Not Our Enemy" campaign, which argues the United States should pursue cooperation with Beijing rather than confrontation. House Ways and Means Committee Republicans have accused the group of promoting narratives aligned with Chinese Communist Party interests, allegations CodePink denies.

Asked why campaigns such as CodePink's "China Is Not Our Enemy" matter, Johnson said they promote an image of China that serves Beijing's strategic interests by downplaying the broader geopolitical competition between the two countries.

"The idea that we don't want war with China, we want peace... these are all noble goals," Johnson said. "But... its strategic function is that it masks the fact that Beijing actually does seek a world order that is more shaped by Beijing in which the United States plays a lesser role."

Johnson said China does not have to convince Americans to support the Chinese Communist Party to advance its interests. Instead, he said, Beijing benefits when public debate shifts away from viewing China as a strategic competitor.

"The real issue is whether there is actually a balance and whether we have enough transparency to allow us to assess whether there's a balance," Johnson said.

Fox News' Asra Q. Nomani contributed to this report.

item.title: Attempted Trump assassin Thomas Crooks used 'Bob Dole' alias before anonymous donor paid for cremation: docs

item.content:encoded:

item.title: Mr T taught me a lesson every kid on Chicago's South Side needs to hear
item.description: From Robert Taylor Homes to Lake Forest, Mr. T's life proves that faith, hard work and self-respect can overcome even the toughest circumstances.
item.content:encoded:
I recently watched the new Netflix documentary on Mr. T. I admit it was disappointing. It felt thin and rushed to me. The filmmakers clearly had no passion for the film since it failed to capture his nature, his complexities, his faith, his service, the hardships and the depth of the road that he traveled. A 48-minute documentary is not enough to do justice to such a life. After all, this is a man who traveled from the rough and violent housing projects known as the Robert Taylor Homes to the top of the world.

Still, the documentary reminded me of why Mr. T has always been such an inspirational figure in my life, from my childhood even to now. I hold him up as a role model to my young kids at Project H.O.O.D. His life is one of hard work, doing the right thing and having a dream. Those are not clichés or empty slogans. They are the values that create opportunities in life.

Laurence Tureaud was born May 21, 1952, the second-youngest of 12 children on Chicago’s South Side. His father, a minister, left when Laurence was five. His mother, Willie, earned a living cleaning houses in the Lake Forest area of Chicago, and her income to support all her children was supplemented by an $87 monthly welfare check. They were poor, but not in family or spirit. Mr. T talks of how they went to church, loved their mother and stayed away from the gangs.

MR. T ON FAITH: 'I ANSWER ONLY TO GOD'

One of my favorite Mr. T quotes is, "I was born and raised in the ghetto, but the ghetto was not born and raised in me." Like anyone in the Robert Taylor Homes, he saw violence and all the things that no child should ever see. He also saw racism. He saw white men call his father a "boy." 

In the documentary, he talks of how his brother went to fight in Vietnam as a Marine and came home only to be called a "boy." When Laurence was 18, he vowed that no one would ever call him a boy. He changed his name to Mr. T so that the first word out of anyone talking to him would be "Mister." What he was demanding was the respect and dignity that his family had been denied. He respected himself.

WHO IS RAISING AMERICA'S CHILDREN? MENTOR WARNS KIDS ARE SEEKING ROLE MODELS ONLINE AS COMMUNITIES FADE

At Dunbar Vocational High School, he became a football star and a city wrestling champion. He did not have a fancy gym to build his muscles. He worked out with his brothers on the concrete around the projects. They did push-ups. They did chin-ups from tree branches. They wrestled one another. They built those muscles the honest way. Mr. T won a scholarship to Prairie View A&M, but that did not work out. He moved to the Loop of Chicago because that is where the money was. For me, that is key because he put himself where the opportunity was. He wound up working three jobs at once, and one of them was as a bouncer at a club.

It was there that he got the news that his mother had been robbed of her welfare money by thugs in the elevator of the projects. They told her to give them her money or they would cut her throat. Mr. T grabbed his shotgun and went into the projects, where he confronted gang members until he found the people who had made his mother fear for her life. After confronting those responsible, he decided to become a bodyguard. He would protect others the way he believed he had failed to protect his mother.

THE WELFARE STATE BROKE BLACK FAMILIES. WORK CAN HELP RESTORE THE DREAM

What I love about this story is that he turned what he believed to be a personal failure into a calling. I don’t think it was a personal failure at all, but what he was trying to do in his own way was make the world a better place. He would use his talents and smarts in that way. He didn’t fall into the gang life or anything like that. He created a new pathway in life instead.

I don’t know where I read it, but I remember the story of when he was nine years old or so. He told his mother, "One of these days I’m going to be big and strong. I’m going to be a football player and a boxer. I’m going to buy you a beautiful house and pretty dresses." She didn’t laugh at him or mock him. She didn’t doubt him. She instead spoke to him of values and told him that the way to get there was to work hard, save his money and get after it. That’s what Mr. T did. It was those values, not the Hollywood fame, not the gold chains, not the "I pity the fool" line — it was those values that were the engine of his life.

NEW STUDY REVEALS THE SINGLE MOST CRITICAL FACTOR IN WHETHER CHILDREN KEEP THEIR FAITH INTO ADULTHOOD

That’s the part that I want my kids to hear. Not the mohawk or the tough scowl. I tell them that Mr. T was once just a child like them, born into a bad ZIP code. But he was a dreamer who had family around him and who never walked down the wrong path or went to jail because he could not bear to break his mother’s heart. That’s how love can save a child.

And I tell them how Mr. T started at the bottom. He didn’t look for shortcuts or get-rich-quick schemes. He believed in himself, and he created his own opportunities. He used sports to discipline himself, he served his country, and he worked as a janitor, gym teacher and a doorman before anyone called him a "star." He stayed true to himself and made himself so unique that people just wanted to be around him. He was one of a kind and, most of all, he was real, and that’s why the world gravitated toward him.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

We spend far too much time telling the young kids on the South Side that the system or the Man is out to get them. We talk about systemic racism without going anywhere. There’s no hope in any of that. That’s why those conversations just peter out and die when we run out of doom and gloom. And what good does it do to poison a young child’s mind with all that negativity?

That’s why I’d rather talk about South Side heroes like Mr. T. His life gives us the simple but brutally honest lesson: Your circumstances are real, and they may be unfair and stacked against you, but they are not your destiny. You are. Your faith, your work, your respect and the dream that you have for yourself — that is your destiny. You have to do the hardest thing in the world, which is to believe in yourself. If you do, you will reach heights you never knew were possible.

That is the simple truth I tell my kids every day. I even tell that to myself. I know I speak of opportunity all the time, but it is not a political talking point for me. It is the lifesaver. It is the boy who decides that he will buy his mother a house. It is the young man who decides that his circumstances will not define him. It is the man who decides his fate. I pity the fool who looks at Mr. T’s life and still tells our kids they cannot rise.

And, yes, Mr. T did buy his mother a beautiful mansion, complete with an elevator, in the Lake Forest neighborhood where she used to clean houses.

item.title: Oil squeeze tightens as Iran-backed attacks cripple Hormuz escape routes
item.description: A drone attack damaged Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline as Houthi rebels seize strategic islands near Bab el-Mandeb, squeezing oil routes beyond Hormuz.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. is choking off Iran’s oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz. But the routes meant to shield other Gulf producers from that disruption are now coming under pressure themselves.

A drone attack last week badly damaged Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, a critical bypass that carries crude oil across the kingdom to the Red Sea. Repairs could leave it largely out of service for three to five weeks after it had been moving roughly 2.6 million to 4 million barrels per day in recent weeks.

At the same time, Iran-backed Houthi rebels have seized additional territory and strategic islands around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean — adding pressure to another major shipping route already battered by years of attacks.

And those repeated disruptions are already reaching American consumers.

NEW RISK FOR US CONSUMERS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS THREATEN A SECOND MAJOR OIL CHOKEPOINT

U.S. diesel prices hit a record national average of $6.23 a gallon Monday, according to AAA, while regular gasoline averaged $4.32. Brent crude climbed as high as roughly $110 a barrel during the day.

Washington has sharply curtailed Iran’s oil exports and trade, but the wider conflict is still disrupting energy supplies elsewhere in the region, especially as Iran-backed Houthi rebels strengthen their stance along the coastline in Yemen.

THE OVERLOOKED WAY THE IRAN WAR IS MAKING GROCERIES, AMAZON PACKAGES AND NEW HOMES MORE EXPENSIVE

The question now is whether Iran is hurting enough to make the concessions Trump wants — and how much economic damage Tehran and its allies can still inflict while it holds out.

The economic pressure on Tehran is mounting.

Iran has gone weeks without sending meaningful new crude exports through Hormuz. Since the United States reinstated its naval blockade July 14, no Iranian crude cargoes have successfully crossed the strait to China, Tehran’s largest remaining oil customer, according to Kpler, Vortexa and TankerTrackers.com.

Iranian crude and condensate loadings fell to roughly 220,000 to 255,000 barrels per day in August, down from about 740,000 in July and roughly 2 million in March.

Commercial shipping through Hormuz also remains deeply disrupted. Recent readings from Kpler, which tracks real-time data on global commodity flows and maritime shipping, have repeatedly put visible commodity-vessel transits in the single digits, even as the U.S. has worked to restore some movement through the waterway.

Miad Maleki, a senior fellow with the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said the pressure is increasingly reaching beyond Iran’s oil industry and into the broader economy.

HORMUZ CRISIS HIDES A DEEPER OIL THREAT THAT COULD OUTLAST THE WAR

"There are a series of indications" that the pressure is working, Maleki told Fox News Digital, citing the combined effect of sanctions, the naval blockade and growing diplomatic isolation.

Iran depends heavily on trade through the United Arab Emirates and Turkey, Maleki said, and restrictions on those channels are making it harder to obtain foreign currency and essential imports.

Gasoline could become an especially difficult pressure point.

Iran remains one of the world’s major crude producers but lacks sufficient refining capacity to meet its own demand, leaving it dependent on imports that have become more difficult to secure.

The regime can cushion some of the financial blow by continuing to print currency and pay salaries, Maleki said, allowing inflation to absorb part of the pressure rather than immediately cutting government payrolls.

Physical shortages are harder to solve.

But that does not necessarily mean Tehran has deliberately substituted the Bab el-Mandeb for Hormuz as a new source of leverage.

Iran expert Arash Azizi said Tehran has already been forced to recognize that its ability to dominate the Strait of Hormuz is weaker than it once claimed.

"Iran has realized that some of the leverage it has over the threat of Hormuz is gone," Azizi told Fox News Digital.

"[Iran] is not able to close it effectively and is desperately trying to find a way to better its odds," he said.

Azizi cautioned, however, against treating every Houthi move as part of a coordinated Iranian strategy to transfer pressure from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea.

"Iran has limited control, and the Houthi-Saudi conflict has a dynamics of its own," he said.

IRAN LOSES KEY ECONOMIC LIFELINE IN MIDDLE EAST THAT TRUMP'S SANCTIONS COULDN'T REACH AS DEADLOCK PERSISTS

Iran encourages and materially supports the Houthis, Azizi said, but does not exercise full operational control over the group.

That distinction matters as the Houthis strengthen their position around Bab el-Mandeb.

Their capture of Mayun Island, the port of Mokha and, most recently, the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands has expanded their reach around one of the world’s most important shipping corridors. Yet the group has continued to allow many vessels to pass rather than attempting a total closure of the strait.

Azizi described the instability there as a "double-edged sword" for Tehran.

Pressure on shipping and Saudi energy infrastructure can raise costs for Iran’s adversaries and increase anxiety in global oil markets. But a broader regional conflict can also make it harder for Tehran to achieve what Azizi described as its overriding objective: ending the war, preserving the Islamic Republic and beginning reconstruction.

For Tehran, he said, the immediate goal is therefore less about opening a new front than improving the terms on which it can end the current one.

Iran wants "some sort of a deal that puts an end to the war," preserves the Islamic Republic and allows it to begin postwar reconstruction, Azizi said.

That shifts the central question back to Washington.

The Trump administration has demonstrated that it can inflict severe economic pressure on Iran. What remains unclear is whether additional pressure produces the concessions Washington wants — and whether the costs Iran and its regional allies can still impose improve Tehran’s bargaining position or deepen its isolation.

Azizi believes Tehran may already be prepared to move.

"I think Iran is ready to make concessions," he said. "The question is, what concessions the United States would find acceptable?"

He said Iran’s negotiating position has already softened from earlier in the conflict, when Tehran claimed sweeping authority over traffic through Hormuz.

The regime’s principal red line now, he argued, is its own survival.

Some Iranian officials may still believe continued pressure on energy markets and the U.S. economy could improve Tehran’s hand, particularly ahead of the midterm elections, Azizi said. But the imbalance in economic pain remains stark.

"We are not hurting. Our daily life is not affected in a crazy manner by this war," he said of Americans. "Iran is hurting a lot more than the United States."

"Iran is selling no oil," Azizi added.

Azizi said the blockade, more than the administration’s latest sanctions package alone, has fundamentally worsened Iran’s outlook by restricting trade while leaving businesses with little idea when normal commercial activity might resume.

Maleki similarly said the regime can absorb inflation and financial losses for some time without immediately buckling. The more difficult test comes when financial pressure becomes physical scarcity.

That makes the next phase of the U.S. campaign less about proving that Iran is hurting than determining whether Washington can turn that pain into an acceptable deal before Tehran or its regional allies find new ways to raise the cost of holding out.

"They can keep printing rial," Maleki said. "But they can’t print gasoline."

item.title: Tesla Cybercab bars kids under 13 as scrutiny grows
item.description: Tesla's Cybercab launched in Austin with no steering wheel or pedals, but hidden details about age limits and missing safety features may shock riders.
item.content:encoded:
Tesla's Cybercab is finally carrying riders in Austin, Texas. And some of the details buried in the fine print may surprise you.

The gold two-seater has no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla says it uses cameras and AI to handle the driving, putting passengers entirely in the hands of its autonomous system.

Yet the Sept. 3 launch was unusually low-key for Tesla. The main presentation reportedly lasted about 15 minutes, and Elon Musk apparently did not speak. Then, on Sept. 4, federal safety regulators announced an investigation into how Tesla certified Cybercab for U.S. roads.

Tesla has spent years building toward this moment. Now that real riders are climbing inside, the little details suddenly become much more important. Here is what you should know before you step into a Cybercab.

ZOOX ROBOTAXI REDESIGN BRINGS BIG RIDER UPGRADES

NEW! Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you take a more active role in your healthcare. You’ll learn how to organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare questions for your next doctor’s visit. No technical

experience is needed.

Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com

If you planned to call a Cybercab for a family ride, check the passenger rules first. Tesla says children under 13 cannot ride in Cybercab "at this time." Teens ages 13 through 17 can ride, although an adult must accompany them for the entire trip.

Interestingly, Tesla sets a different age limit for the Model Y vehicles in its Robotaxi service. Children ages 8 through 17 can ride in those vehicles with an adult. Guests under 8 cannot.

So, an 11-year-old could ride in a Tesla Model Y Robotaxi but could not take the same trip in a Cybercab. Tesla does not explain the reason for that difference in its current rider guidance. Then there is another detail parents may notice.

Tesla confirms that Cybercab has no LATCH or ISOFIX child-restraint system. If a rider needs a booster seat, Tesla says it must use a seat belt to secure it.

That may sound odd considering Cybercab does not allow children under 13. However, some older children may still need a booster seat depending on their size and local requirements.

Tesla gives instructions for using one, but there are no LATCH anchors to attach it to. It is the kind of detail most of us probably would not think about until a Cybercab showed up at the curb.

A driverless vehicle still needs a plan for the moment something goes wrong. According to Tesla documentation, a collision can trigger several automatic responses. The airbags can deploy and the doors can unlock. Hazard lights and interior lights can also switch on.

The vehicle can disable its high-voltage battery, move the windows into a vent position and apply the brakes until it comes to a stop. Tesla's system can also open a two-way connection with its Robotaxi Support team.

That support connection could become especially important in a vehicle where nobody can grab the steering wheel or hit the brakes. Tesla also gives riders ways to stop a trip themselves.

UBER LETS PARENTS WATCH TEEN RIDES LIVE

Look above you when you get inside a Cybercab. Tesla placed a dedicated Stop button between the dome lights. Pressing it sends an immediate pull-over request, ends the ride and connects you with Robotaxi Support.

You can also tap Pull Over on the touchscreen or make the request through the Robotaxi app. However, Tesla warns that an "immediate" pull-over may still take some time. For example, the vehicle may need longer to reach a safe stopping point while traveling on a highway. That is worth knowing before your first ride.

Tesla's electronic door releases have attracted criticism because passengers may need a mechanical backup when a vehicle loses power.

Cybercab still uses electronically controlled doors during normal operation. In fact, the nearest door can open automatically when the ride requester approaches.

Inside, you can normally open the door through the touchscreen or gently lift a lever on the door panel. Pull that lever firmly all the way up, though, and it activates the mechanical release. Both Cybercab doors have one.

I like that Tesla put the emergency release where a passenger can actually see and reach it. There is one important warning. Tesla says using the mechanical release can damage the window or trim. If the vehicle has no power and the window remains fully raised, Tesla warns the glass could shatter when someone activates the release. That is one instruction I would want to know before an emergency.

Tesla also made a major change underneath the vehicle. Cybercab uses a brake-by-wire system rather than a traditional hydraulic setup. Electronic actuators control the brake calipers instead of hydraulic lines carrying brake fluid.

Musk said in a post on X that electric brakes avoid the complexity of routing hydraulic plumbing around the vehicle. Tesla has already used steer-by-wire technology in the Cybertruck.

With Cybercab, passengers have no physical driving controls at all. That puts even more responsibility on the electronics and software to work properly every time.

Here is one of the stranger details Tesla included in its new rider guide. Cybercab passengers can lower the windows, but Tesla says they "cannot be fully opened at this time." The company does not explain why.

The window switches also sit underneath the center touchscreen rather than on the doors. So, yes, you can crack a window for some air. You simply cannot roll it all the way down right now.

WAYMO RECALLS ROBOTAXIS OVER CONSTRUCTION-ZONE RISK

At least you should have somewhere to plug in your devices. Tesla confirms that Cybercab has USB-C charging ports inside the cabin.

An attendee at the launch reported that those ports can deliver up to 90 watts of power. That could be enough to charge many laptops.

However, Tesla's current public rider guide does not list that wattage. So, I would treat the 90-watt figure as an early report until Tesla publishes the specification itself.

On Sept. 3, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened what it calls an Audit Query into Tesla's certification that Cybercab meets all applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards. NHTSA announced the action on Sept. 4 following the vehicle's commercial deployment in Austin.

Automakers in the U.S. generally certify their own vehicles as complying with federal standards. NHTSA can then audit those certifications and investigate when questions come up.

Cybercab presents an unusual case because it has no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors. Many federal vehicle rules were written around cars designed for human drivers. NHTSA's audit reportedly covers about 1,000 Cybercabs as the agency reviews how Tesla determined the vehicles comply.

That does not mean regulators have found Cybercab unsafe. It does mean Tesla now has to back up its certification with technical information that satisfies the agency.

If you get the chance to ride in a Cybercab, I would spend a minute learning the cabin before the car starts moving. Find the emergency Stop button. Know where the mechanical door release sits. Keep your seat belt fastened for the entire trip.

Tesla says every passenger must buckle up before the ride begins. Cybercab may pull over or cancel a trip if it detects improper seat-belt use. Parents should also pay close attention to the age rules. Cybercab and Tesla's Model Y Robotaxi do not follow the same limits.

Beyond that, remember how new this vehicle is. Tesla is putting a very different kind of car into real-world service, and regulators are already asking questions about how it fits existing safety standards.

We have seen how unexpected situations can challenge other autonomous vehicles too. CyberGuy recently reported how Waymo recalled robotaxis over a construction-zone risk after vehicles entered closed freeway construction areas.

The technology can be impressive. Still, the real test comes when these vehicles deal with everything ordinary roads throw at them.

Cybercab is finally moving from Tesla's big promise to something people can actually ride in. I like seeing safeguards such as the mechanical door release and emergency Stop button, especially when passengers have no steering wheel or pedals to grab. Still, the under-13 restriction, lack of LATCH anchors and windows that do not fully open caught my attention. Add the federal investigation, and Tesla now has something bigger to prove. Putting Cybercab on the road is one thing. Showing that people can trust it day after day is the real test.

Would you climb into a Cybercab today with no steering wheel or pedals, or would you want to see a longer safety record before trusting it with your ride? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

item.title: Dan Lanning spars with reporter after Dante Moore misses media following Oregon's loss to Oklahoma State
item.description: Dan Lanning defended Dante Moore's postgame absence, saying the Oregon Ducks quarterback needed two IVs for dehydration after the stunning loss.
item.content:encoded:
The Oregon Ducks suffered the most shocking loss of the young college football season by falling to Oklahoma State 39-31 in Week 2. Senior quarterback Dante Moore was nowhere to be found during media availability following the Ducks' loss on the road, which was noticed by every reporter in the room, but according to head coach Dan Lanning, his absence was excused.

The way in which Lanning explained the situation with Moore, however, has led to quite the reaction among fans.

The 40-year-old shared that his quarterback was dehydrated after the final whistle in Stillwater, Okla., before alluding to that being the cause of his absence during the postgame media scrum.

item.title: NATO jets shoot down drone in Lithuanian airspace as Russia grows 'increasingly reckless,' Rutte says
item.description: Two Italian Eurofighter Typhoons scrambled under NATO command and downed a drone over Lithuania that officials say likely came from Belarus.
item.content:encoded:
Two Italian Eurofighter Typhoons operating under NATO command scrambled overnight and shot down a drone over Lithuania, marking the first time a drone has been downed in the Baltic nation's airspace, officials said Tuesday.

The incident came less than a day after NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte warned that strikes close to alliance territory would drive the 32-nation bloc to increase its support for Ukraine.

The drone was destroyed near the village of Pratkūnai, about 60 miles northwest of the capital, Vilnius.

RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS

"Last night, two Italian Eurofighters deployed on NATO Air Defence mission at Siauliai, scrambled and shot down a drone over Lithuanian airspace," a NATO official told Fox News Digital. "The operation was coordinated through NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre in Uedem, Germany. Investigations are ongoing together with national authorities."

Lithuanian officials said the drone most likely entered from neighboring Belarus and remained in the country's airspace for about 30 minutes before it was intercepted.

Lithuanian Air Force Commander Antanas Matutis said the recovered drone was "likely" carrying explosives.

Authorities are examining the wreckage of the downed drone to determine its origin and purpose.

The incident comes amid heightened tensions along NATO's eastern flank.

RUSSIA EXPOSES NATO WEAPONS GAP AS TOP COMMANDER WARNS ‘THE MATH IS NOT IN FAVOR OF THE WEST’

Speaking in Brussels on Monday, Rutte said strikes "close to NATO territory" showed Russian President Vladimir Putin's "desperation and also his desire to sow fear and terror."

"Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine," Rutte said, while pledging to strengthen NATO defenses along its eastern flank.

In a separate incident Tuesday, Denmark said a Russian frigate fired flares toward a Danish military helicopter conducting routine surveillance over the Baltic Sea. Denmark summoned the Russian ambassador over the encounter.

Meanwhile, Russia continued drone strikes across Ukraine, killing three people in Kyiv, Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, according to Ukrainian officials.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv remained ready to support de-escalation if the U.S. could ensure Russia was prepared to stop its attacks. Ukrainian forces also struck an oil refinery in Syzran and targeted a drone production facility in Taganrog, he said.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Nike-linked CoachingHER program faces scrutiny over gender bias training and definition of girls
item.description: Sarah Barker claims Nike-backed CoachingHER program defines "girls" to include transgender athletes while retraining coaches on gender bias.
item.content:encoded:
Nike helped create a coaching program designed to keep girls in sports.

Three years later, the program is expanding into college classrooms and through a partnership with a national sports governing body, while its own FAQ defines "girls" to include anyone under 18 who identifies as one.

Sarah Barker, a former coach and creator of The Female Category, spent months reviewing CoachingHER, its training modules and the research cited to support them. She told OutKick in an exclusive interview that what she found does not match how she believes the program is being presented to coaches.

"Everything about it tells me that it is not, in fact, what it is being sold as," Barker said.

NIKE SHAREHOLDERS REJECT TRANSPARENCY PROPOSAL AS FAITH-BASED FIRM QUESTIONS DEI COMMITMENTS

CoachingHER launched in 2023 as a collaboration between Nike and the Tucker Center for Research on Girls & Women in Sport at the University of Minnesota.

Nike said at the time that it developed the free digital resource to help coaches recognize unconscious gender biases and stereotypes that negatively affect girls' experiences in sports.

Barker first encountered CoachingHER through the Minnesota State High School League after spending 10 years as a coach.

She decided to take the course herself.

"I did the training modules and I interviewed the director of the Coaching Her program at the Tucker Center," Barker said.

Then she kept digging.

CoachingHER’s current FAQ defines "girls" as someone under 18 "who was assigned female at birth or who identifies as a girl" and says the program is "inclusive of gender-expansive identities," language Barker said was displayed more prominently when she first investigated the program in 2024.

For Barker, those few words change the meaning of the training that follows.

The CoachingHER website says its courses give coaches "girl-centered strategies" and tools to create "supportive, inclusive environments for girls in sports."

Barker said that definition becomes especially important in a module addressing bodies and identities.

"They exhort coaches in one of the training modules to accept all, and all is in capital letters, all bodies and identities," Barker said.

MEGAN RAPINOE'S LATEST DEFENSE OF MALES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS COLLAPSES UNDER ITS OWN HYPOCRISY | DAN ZAKSHESKE

On its face, Barker said much of the advice sounds unobjectionable. But she argues the program's definition of "girls" changes the context because it also encompasses transgender-identifying athletes.

Barker's broader criticism is that CoachingHER's emphasis on coaches' gender biases does not match what she found in the research on why girls leave sports.

A current CoachingHER article, citing 2024 research from Dove and Nike, says low body confidence is the "No. 1 reason girls quit sports." But the program describes its mission as addressing "the unconscious gender biases and stereotypes held by coaches."

The Tucker Center and Nike have said coaches were chosen as a focus because earlier research identified them as an important influence on girls' sports experiences. In a 2023 article about the creation of CoachingHER, Tucker Center director Nicole LaVoi and former Nike social-impact executive Caitlin Morris also said workshops with girls and coaches helped shape the program's focus on gender stereotypes.

Barker argues that explanation does not resolve the disconnect she found in the research on why girls actually leave sports.

"They knew that the number one reason girls drop out of sports was concerns with body image," Barker said.

She said CoachingHER director Alicia Pelton acknowledged the same point when Barker interviewed her in 2024.

Yet Barker said that in the research and lists of dropout factors she reviewed, coaches' gender bias and their understanding of gender identity were not identified among the leading reasons girls leave sports.

"What's weird about this is that of the many reasons listed for girls dropping out of sports, their coaches' gender bias was never listed, not in the Tucker Center's own research," Barker said. "It was never listed, not even in the top 15 reasons."

That led Barker to question why a program marketed as a way to keep girls in sports was focused so heavily on changing coaches' attitudes about gender.

"Why would they build an entire program around blaming coaches when they know that that is not true?" she said.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

When Nike publicly announced the program in March 2023, the company said it had developed CoachingHER in partnership with the Tucker Center.

Nike's website continues to promote CoachingHER in 2026, describing it as a resource "created in partnership with the Tucker Center for Research on Girls and Women in Sport."

The CoachingHER website also continues to display Nike's logo under the words "Brought to you by."

Barker said she separately discussed Nike's involvement with CoachingHER program director Alicia Pelton during her 2024 investigation.

"When I interviewed Alicia Pelton ... she was open about the fact that Nike funded this program," Barker said. "I don't know the amount. I asked and was not told the amount."

WOMEN’S SPORTS MEDIA OUTLET BACKS TRANS ATHLETES, THEN AVOIDS QUESTIONS FROM REPORTER WHO DISAGREES

While Nike’s current financial involvement with CoachingHER is unclear, its public connection to the program remains. In January 2026, the University of Minnesota described CoachingHER as "powered by Nike."

OutKick asked Nike whether it currently funds CoachingHER, what role the company currently plays in developing or reviewing the curriculum, and whether Nike endorses the program's definition of girls.

OutKick also contacted the Tucker Center and CoachingHER seeking responses to Barker's criticisms and clarification about Nike's current role in the program.

Neither Nike nor the Tucker Center responded before publication.

Since Barker first investigated CoachingHER in 2024, the program has expanded beyond youth coaches.

The Tucker Center's Educational Champions initiative encourages professors and institutions to incorporate individual CoachingHER modules or full courses into subjects including coaching education, sports psychology, gender studies, athlete development and physical education.

In May, USA Weightlifting announced a partnership with the Tucker Center that gives eligible members access to CoachingHER courses through its learning platform. USA Weightlifting described the training as a way to help coaches "recognize and reduce unconscious gender bias" and build environments that support girls' participation and long-term success.

Barker believes coaches are being taught to view biological sex differences through the lens of gender bias while being told the program's purpose is to protect girls' opportunities in sports.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Barker calls that "girl washing."

"Girl washing is calling something beneficial to girls, when in fact it's actually harmful to girls," she said.

CoachingHER says its mission is to reduce gender inequalities in sports by helping coaches challenge unconscious gender biases and stereotypes.

Barker said she shares CoachingHER’s stated goal of keeping girls in sports. Her objection is to the program’s definition of "girls" and what she believes follows from it.

"This is a group of people that's going to need a lot of re-education, a lot of heavy-duty indoctrination," Barker said of coaches who maintain sex-based distinctions in girls' sports.

"That is what Coaching Her is. It is an indoctrination program for coaches ... to normalize boys in girls sports," she added.

"It is not about girls, it is not about keeping girls in sports at all," she said. "What's really galling is that they're lying about it and getting away with it by calling this beneficial."

"It is the opposite of beneficial."

Kramer is charged with receiving a firearm and ammunition, knowing or having reasonable cause to believe they would be used to commit a felony or federal crime of terrorism, including providing or attempting to provide material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization.

FBI ARRESTS WOMAN WHO ALLEGEDLY PLOTTED ISIS-LINKED ATTACK ON NEW YORK STATE CAPITOL BUILDING

Agents approached him when he returned to the hotel carrying two bags from the store. Searches of Kramer, his hotel room and his home turned up a semiautomatic rifle, five rifle magazines — two loaded and three capable of holding 30 rounds each — and 190 rounds of rifle ammunition, according to the complaint.

Agents also found a rifle scope and bipod, an entrenchment tool, pepper spray and about 30 knives. A handwritten note read, "DoNt look For me[.] IDK what I did buT I cant live In constant Fear[.]"

Attorney General Todd Blanche said the arrest came as Americans marked the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.

"Their outstanding work thwarted this alleged attack before innocent lives could be lost," Blanche said.

FBI Director Kash Patel said Kramer had been "plotting a violent attack in support of ISIS," citing his online activity and acquisition of weapons.

The Justice Department did not identify a specific target for the alleged attack.

Kramer was booked into the Butler County Jail and made his first court appearance Monday. Prosecutors have asked that he be held without bond, arguing that he poses a danger to the community.

item.title: Kash Patel to tout 'largest' year-to-year violent crime drop in US history
item.description: FBI Director Kash Patel is set to tell senators the FBI delivered historic crime reductions, disrupted terrorist plots, captured top fugitives and overhauled the bureau under his leadership.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: FBI Director Kash Patel is set to tell lawmakers Tuesday that the FBI and its law enforcement partners have achieved what he calls the "most prolific run of crime reduction in United States history," according to his prepared opening remarks for the Senate Judiciary Committee's annual FBI oversight hearing.

In his opening statement obtained by Fox News Digital, Patel will highlight the achievements before the Senate Judiciary Committee, which will focus on recent changes within the FBI.

The results include a major drop in murder rates, crackdowns on drug and human trafficking, successful efforts to thwart terrorist attacks and the apprehension of top fugitives.

According to his prepared statement, Patel attributes the gains to the Trump administration, saying the agency could not have achieved them without the administration's support.

FBI BOSS KASH PATEL DETAILS HOW AGENCY AND PARTNERS SECURED RECORD-SHATTERING FIFA WORLD CUP

"In 2025, according to the Uniform Crime Report, we delivered the LARGEST year to year reduction of violent crime in AMERICAN HISTORY," Patel's statement reads.

"They happened with an administration that BACKS the BLUE and a new FBI that has been REBUILT to crush violent threats BEFORE they harm Americans."

According to the FBI's figures, the national murder rate fell 20% over the previous 18 months while violent crime arrests increased 90% and violent criminal and gang member arrests rose 30%.

Just this weekend, the FBI disrupted a terrorist attack near Pittsburgh, according to Patel’s prepared statement. The suspect allegedly purchased a firearm and indicated online that he intended to carry out a violent attack on behalf of ISIS.

In total, about 1,039 individuals were thwarted from executing terrorist attacks, according to Patel's statement. The individuals are among more than 4,260 arrests tied to Foreign Terrorist Organizations (FTOs).

Those efforts also included securing major national events, such as the 2026 FIFA World Cup, the Grand Prix and UFC 250 without a single major security incident.

FBI CAPTURES TOP TEN MOST WANTED FUGITIVE WITH ALLEGED SINALOA CARTEL TIES, PATEL SAYS

Patel is expected to announce at Tuesday's hearing the capture of Anibal Alexander Canelon Aguirre in Venezuela, making him the 10th FBI "Ten Most Wanted" fugitive nabbed during Patel's tenure.

According to Patel's prepared statement, the FBI has now captured 10 fugitives from its "Ten Most Wanted" list — more than 2.5 times the number apprehended during the previous four years combined.

Aguirre, according to the FBI, led "a large international conspiracy to steal millions of dollars from financial institutions in support of the Tren de Aragua, through an ATM jackpotting scheme since at least 2024."

Patel will also highlight that the FBI seized more than 3,258 kilograms of fentanyl, identified about 11,000 child victims and arrested more than 5,000 child predators and human traffickers.

Patel's prepared statement credits the historic transformation in American public safety and agency accountability to aggressive law enforcement, technological modernization, including artificial intelligence and operational efficiency.

"We expanded our use of artificial intelligence by 605 percent to accelerate threat detection, triage, analysis, and processing," the statement reads.

PATEL SAYS FBI HAS CUT BUREAUCRACY, MOVED 1,000 AGENTS TO FIELD OFFICES IN 'GENERATIONAL' OVERHAUL

Patel is expected to tell lawmakers that the FBI eliminated a multi-year backlog of 1.8 million lab samples while saving more than $300 million through spending and facilities reviews.

"As we recently announced, the FBI’s Lab Division had a backlog of over 1.8 million samples that had existed for years prior to my confirmation… As of last month, that backlog is now ZERO," Patel's statement reads.

Patel will also highlight internal bureau reforms that shifted more than 1,000 agents and staff into field operations, along with the opening of a new field office in Billings, Montana, as part of the FBI's expansion in Indian Country through Operation Steadfast Promise.

item.title: Island getaway hit with urgent warning as hurricane damage leaves travelers without power
item.description: Derek Kawakami, mayor of Kaua'i, says the Hawaiian island is still digging itself out of the mud after Hurricane Lowell and discourages tourists from visiting.
item.content:encoded:
Tourists are being urged to hold off on visiting a scenic Hawaiian island as it continues to recover from a devastating hurricane.

Kaua'i, one of Hawaii's westernmost islands, was battered by Hurricane Lowell on Sept. 7 and 8, which brought severe winds, heavy rain and widespread power outages.

As of Monday, the island was still recovering, with electricity restored to about 82% of customers, according to Kaua'i County officials.

VACATION PARADISE EVACUATED AS RAGING WILDFIRE THREATENS TO ROAR BACK AMID HIGH WINDS

Speaking to reporters just a few days ago, Kaua'i County Mayor Derek Kawakami discouraged tourists from visiting and said the island was still digging itself "out of the mud."

The mayor added that Kaua'i would "gladly welcome" tourists once the island "recover[s] to a point where we can handle more capacity coming in," according to Kaua'i Now News.

"We are going to recover faster than I think we anticipated," he added, though he did not specify when the island might be ready to welcome visitors back.

The Hawai'i Tourism Authority (HTA) also posted an advisory late last week asking visitors to reconsider their trips.

US WARNS AMERICANS TO AVOID VACATION HOT SPOT AMID QUAKE FALLOUT AND VIOLENT CRIME

"As the island focuses its resources on immediate needs, the Hawai'i Tourism Authority encourages travelers with upcoming Kaua'i plans to reschedule or consider visiting another Hawaiian island instead of canceling their trip," the organization stated.

"Travelers who are rescheduling should check directly with their airline, accommodations, and other travel providers for updated options."

Fox News Digital reached out to Mayor Kawakami's office for comment.

Also known as the Garden Island, Kaua'i is the fourth largest of Hawaii's main islands.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

The island received nearly 1.42 million visitors in 2025, according to Hawaii's Department of Business, Economic Development & Tourism (DBEDT).

The tourist destination is known for its picturesque landscape and coastline, including Nā Pali Coast, Waimea Canyon and Hanalei Bay.

Hawaii's tourism industry has faced a series of natural hazards this year.

Earlier this year, Hawaii health officials issued brown water advisories across multiple islands after a storm brought heavy rain and contaminated runoff.

In January, Hawaii's Kilauea volcano erupted, leading officials at Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park to warn visitors about heavy traffic, crowds and potential hazards.
